title: Food from the land: where to start
summary: Food is the lowest priority, so spend effort where it pays. Fish are usually more plentiful than game and are caught quietly; small animals are more plentiful than deer; deer are harder to get, and tree stand falls and dragging are their dangers. Never go alone, tell someone where you are going, and have a way to keep meat cool before you take an animal. Wild plants only from the safe list. Insects only cooked, and not by anyone allergic to shellfish. Every page in this category is linked at the end.
doFirst: Spend effort where it pays: the table below shows what each kind of food gives and what it costs.
Never go out alone if you can help it, and tell someone where you are going and when you will be back (American Heart Association, NYS DEC).
This app’s suggestion: start with what your group knows best, fishing. Fish are usually more plentiful than mammals, and catching them is mostly silent (US Army ATP 3-50.21).
Before you take any animal, have a way to keep the meat cool (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife), and know how to dress and cool it (linked below).
After fallout, see Game, fish, milk and gardens after fallout before you use any wild game or fish.

blocks.p: This category is written for a group with some fishing and hunting experience and little or no trapping. Its first job is to show where effort pays in each season and what can hurt you; its second is to make sure an animal, once taken, becomes safe food and is not wasted.
From Wild plants: “Food is the lowest priority: you can survive about three weeks without it. Don’t spend energy or risk poisoning chasing it early.”
In normal times New York requires licences and sets seasons and legal methods for hunting, fishing and trapping. They are all in one place, New York rules.

blocks.p: What the sources say. No source opened gives calories or amounts of meat to compare, so this app gives none. Swipe sideways to see the whole table.

head: Food
What it gives
Effort and risk
rows: A good source of protein and fat; usually more plentiful than mammals (US Army ATP 3-50.21)
Catching them is mostly silent (ATP 3-50.21). Cold water and thin ice are the dangers (NYS DEC)
Concentrate on smaller animals unless you get the chance at large game: there are more of them (US Army FM 21-76)
Zone-of-fire safety in a group (Maine hunter education); gloves with rabbits, hares and rodents (Field dressing game)
Mammals are excellent sources of protein (ATP 3-50.21)

Large game roams vast areas and is harder to get (FM 21-76). Falls from tree stands (NYS DEC); dragging can bring on a heart attack (American Heart Association); the bigger the animal, the more it can hurt you (FM 21-76)
Traps work 24 hours a day with no one there (ATP 3-50.21); several well-placed traps can catch much more than one hunter with a rifle (FM 21-76)
Your group has little trapping experience. In normal times New York limits which traps are legal (New York rules)
Deadly look-alikes: eat only what Wild plants lists as safe
Many are 65 to 80 percent protein, against about 20 percent for beef (ATP 3-50.21, FM 21-76)
You need a great many to equal the protein of one rabbit (ATP 3-50.21). Allergy risk (below)

sections.h: By season in Central New York

blocks.p: What the sources say about when each food is there. Where a source is from outside New York, it is named. Hunting, fishing and trapping seasons in normal times are in New York rules.

list: Spring: young dandelion leaves, before the plant flowers, and young cattail shoots (Wild plants). Fish gather at inlets before they spawn, usually in spring or fall; crappie move into shallow water to spawn, and walleye spawn in April in fast-flowing streams (NYS DEC).

Summer: wild raspberries usually ripen in July, blackberries a little later (Wild plants). Small ponds full of sunfish are the best place to get a bite; in summer crappie go to deeper, cooler water (NYS DEC). Squirrels move much less at midday on hot, humid days (Missouri Department of Conservation). Heat spoils meat fast: don’t hunt on a hot day without a way to keep the meat cool (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife).
Fall: fish gather at inlets again (NYS DEC). In Missouri, rabbit numbers are often higher in October (Missouri Department of Conservation).

Winter: ice fishing for yellow perch, sunfish, chain pickerel and northern pike in ponds and lakes, and walleye and lake trout in deep lakes (NYS DEC); the ice rules are under Safety below. Rabbits may move at midday on a sunny day after a cold snap (Missouri Department of Conservation). Cold helps keep meat, but read what the agencies say in Keeping game meat first.

steps: Take stock of what the group owns and knows. The kit list below is a start.
Fish first: it is what your group knows best (this app’s suggestion), and fish are usually more plentiful than game and caught quietly (US Army ATP 3-50.21).
Before anyone hunts, set up a way to keep meat cool (New Jersey Fish and Wildlife) and read Field dressing game, including the signs that an animal is not safe to eat.
Hunt the smaller animals unless you have the chance at a deer (US Army FM 21-76): Small game and birds.
Learn the plants on the safe list in person before you rely on them (Wild plants).

list: Nobody alone. Never hunt alone if you can help it (American Heart Association); use the buddy system on the ice (NYS DEC); on the water, hunt with a companion within sight or call (Minnesota DNR).

Heavy work: dragging a deer can leave even a fit hunter breathless and could bring on a heart attack or stroke (American Heart Association). The American Heart Association says a good health check-up before the hunting season would be ideal. This app’s caution: anyone with heart trouble, or who gets chest pain with effort, does not do the dragging.
In normal times New York requires hunter education for a hunting licence: see New York rules. The hunting pages here assume that training.
During a fallout shelter period, going out at all is ruled by How long to stay in. This app’s caution, from Water and food after fallout: don’t use wild game and fish until officials say you can.
Who should not eat it, from Field dressing game: “Children and anyone who could become pregnant should not eat game shot with lead.”
Be sure of your target and what lies beyond it (NYS DEC). The rest is in Hunting deer and big game and Small game and birds.
Tree stands: a full-body harness, connected before your feet leave the ground and until you are back down (NYS DEC).

Ice: NYS DEC’s general rule is a minimum of 3 to 4 inches (8 to 10 cm) of solid ice; 4 inches (10 cm) to go out on foot; stay off ice 2 inches (5 cm) or thinner. Slush ice is about half as strong; double the thickness for white ice. Check the ice as you go, and carry ice picks (NYS DEC). This app goes by 4 inches on foot.
Boats: wear a life jacket, and dress for the water temperature, not the air (Minnesota DNR).

blocks.p: Someone hurt? A gunshot, a fall from a tree stand, cold water: use the protocols.

blocks.label: Animal or human bite (and rabies risk)

blocks.p: Many insects are 65 to 80 percent protein, against about 20 percent for beef, but you have to gather a great many to get as much protein as one rabbit gives (US Army ATP 3-50.21, 2018).

list: Stick to grasshoppers and crickets, and only to bugs you can easily identify (Michigan State University Extension, which also names sowbugs and pillbugs).
Never eat adult insects that bite or sting, hairy or brightly coloured insects, hairy caterpillars, insects with a strong smell, spiders, or ticks, flies and mosquitoes (ATP 3-50.21).
Collect only where no pesticides have been used (Michigan State University Extension).
Take off stingers, legs, wings and heads (ATP 3-50.21).

Cook every one completely, to kill germs and parasites. A thermometer is hard to use on something so small: stir them in the pan for about 10 minutes on medium heat, and be extra sure they are thoroughly cooked (Michigan State University Extension). Cook any insect collected in the wild; never eat one raw (Ohio State University Extension). The US Army manual FM 21-76 says most insects can be eaten raw; this app goes by the extension services.

blocks.warn: Anyone allergic to shrimp, lobster or other shellfish should not eat insects (Michigan State University Extension; FDA, quoted by Ohio State University Extension), nor anyone allergic to mushrooms (Michigan State University Extension).
